V. Refugees and the environment

Refugees and internally displaced persons are forced to flee because of violations of peace, including armed conflict, internal disturbances and environmental disasters, as well as combined factors. Some may flee because of persecution due to their peace activism, including conscientious objection to participation in war. The hosting of refugees is an important element of solidarity for peace. Refugees often become peace activists, calling for the restoration of peace in their homelands, and seek to be included in peace processes after the end of war.34

Colombia, Germany, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Türkiye and Uganda are considered to be the countries that have shown most solidarity for peace in hosting refugees.35 The Islamic Republic of Iran has gender equality initiatives in joint projects with UNHCR that enable Afghan refugee women to engage in vocational training and employment opportunities. Such initiatives reduce structural violence and contribute to the promotion of positive peace.

Brazil reported that it had launched an innovative voluntary internal relocation programme in response to the influx of Venezuelan nationals through its northern border. It promotes relocation through labour insertion and promotes solidarity by engaging municipalities nationwide in the shared responsibility of protection and integration, thereby promoting social cohesion. Further, it has a community sponsorship programme, whereby civil society groups, faith-based organizations and other community entities assume the role of sponsoring and integrating refugee families into the social fabric, demonstrating a commitment to burden-sharing and deepening the partnership between the State and civil society to safeguard the protection of refugees and migrants.

Brazil also has the Bolsa Verde programme, which provides income support to socioeconomically vulnerable families living in environmentally protected areas. It seeks to encourage ecosystem conservation, promote the sustainable use of natural resources and reduce socioenvironmental conflicts and displacement in order to promote peaceful societies. In addition, its national policy for the protection of human rights defenders and its protection programme for human rights defenders, communicators and environmentalists seek to guarantee the peace of those engaging in environmental protection, social justice and communal rights solidarity actions.

There is concern that the trend towards the externalization of migration and the heavy emphasis on return, revocation of status, use of cessation clauses and elimination of humanitarian protection in both Europe and North America, grounded in xenophobic, unitary solidarity orientations, are eliminating solidarity for refugees and increasing the risk of violence. In contrast, civil society groups, such as Associazione Comunità Papa Giovanni XXIII, support humanitarian corridors, offering safe and legal entry routes for vulnerable people fleeing conflict. Other non-governmental organizations engage in searchand-rescue missions in the Mediterranean, despite being wrongfully subjected to criminal prosecution.36 An additional issue of concern is the fact, reported by several States, that there is a lack of sufficient international financing for demining to enable the return of internally displaced persons and refugees to their place of origin. 34 Maja Janmyr, “Refugees and peace”, in Cecilia M. Bailliet, Research Handbook on International Law and Peace (Cheltenham, Edward Elgar Publishing, 2019). 35 See https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics. 36 See https://www.statewatch.org/news/2023/august/urgent-warning-more-deaths-at-sea-ngo-shipsblocked/; and https://www.msf.org/charges-case-against-rescues-sea-dropped-italy. VI. Countering hate speech, discrimination and violence

There is a trend of disinformation on social media and in political discourse that normalizes hate speech and perpetuates the “othering” of persons of different religions, ethnicities, gender or other collective identity, increasing the risk of incitement to discrimination and/or violence. Some States warned that unchecked racist and revanchist narratives after a peace process could promote a renewed cycle of violence. Civil society groups expressed concern that antisemitism and Islamophobia constituted real threats to the right to peace. Depolarization of solidarity strategies and enforcement mechanisms against incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence should be framed as a form of guaranteeing the right to peace.

The Council of Europe supports a comprehensive approach to combating hate speech as an important element in supporting social peace.37 Similarly, the Rabat Plan of Action on the prohibition of advocacy of national, racial or religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence provides a framework to assess advocacy of national, religious or racial hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence.38 The Organization of Islamic Corporation has monitoring systems to track Islamophobia and discrimination incidents with real-time data collection, as well as operational response systems adapted to emerging challenges and mechanisms to detect early warning signals that could lead to various forms of violence.

Civil society can create spaces for intercultural solidarity dialogues, reconciliation and peaceful coexistence. Civil society organizations engage in a wide variety of solidarity for peace initiatives such as peace walks,39 community-based peace training, interfaith dialogue and social cohesion programmes.40 Solidarity actions in response to terrorist attacks have been described as a type of emotional governance tied to restoring social peace.41 VII. Transition to peace and the participation of vulnerable groups

The equal participation of vulnerable persons in transition to peace processes is an important component of positive peace. Participation should be in good faith and substantive, as noted by the Special Rapporteur on the implications for human rights of the environmentally sound management and disposal of hazardous substances and wastes: “When public participation is reduced to a checklist, instead of being conducive to genuine dialogue, then dialogue is replaced by anger and distrust.”42

As stated by the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, the active involvement of persons with disabilities during all stages of the peace continuum (including prevention, resolution, reconciliation, reconstruction and peacebuilding) is essential. 43 Similarly, the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women has called for the increased participation of women (including Indigenous women, minority women and women with disabilities) in negotiating and mediating peace, peacebuilding and development committees (at the national, State and local levels), in the diplomatic service, in conflict prevention and in the promotion of human rights.44 The Working Group on discrimination 37 See https://rm.coe.int/leaflet-combating-hate-speech-en-november-2022/1680a923f5. 38 See https://www.ohchr.org/en/freedom-of-expression. 39 Submission from Kailash Union. 40 Submission from Kawish Resource Center. 41 Clara Eroukhmanoff, “Responding to terrorism with peace, love and solidarity: ‘Je suis Charlie’, ‘Peace’ and ‘I Heart MCR’”, Journal of International Political Theory, vol. 15, No. 2, March 2019, pp. 167–187. 42 A/HRC/57/52/Add.2, para. 36. 43 CRPD/C/UKR/CO/2-3, para. 65 (d). See also CRPD/C/AZE/CO/2-3, para. 26 (b). 44 See CEDAW/C/THA/CO/8, CEDAW/C/MEX/CO/10, CEDAW/C/TCD/CO/5, CEDAW/C/FJI/CO/6, CEDAW/C/NPL/CO/7, CEDAW/C/NPL/CO/7/Corr.1, CEDAW/C/AFG/CO/4 and CEDAW/C/BWA/CO/5. against women and girls has drawn attention to the failure to include women in peace processes, including their lack of participation at the peace process negotiation table.45

The Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of opinion and expression has also called for the inclusion of women in the process to propose an approach to inclusive peacebuilding.46 The Special Rapporteur on trafficking in persons, especially women and children, has specifically called for action to combat all forms of trafficking in persons to be integrated into peacebuilding measures and into the women and peace and security agenda.47 The Committee on the Rights of the Child has called for the participation of Indigenous children in the peaceful dispute resolution of territorial conflicts and for the creation of complaint mechanisms and awareness campaigns to protect children against hate speech due to their participation in social protests.48

The Working Group of Experts on People of African Descent has warned that the failure of a State to address structural causes of conflict, in particular unequal land distribution and the continued exclusion of people of African descent, is a threat to sustainable peace.49

The Special Rapporteur on the promotion of truth, justice, reparation and guarantees of non-recurrence has called for victims to take part in peace negotiations with armed and/or criminal groups so that the resulting decisions and mechanisms are compatible with their rights to truth, justice and reparation.50 The Special Rapporteur on the human rights of internally displaced persons has called for the participation of internally displaced persons and returnees in national elections in order to promote sustainable reintegration. 51 The Independent Expert on the enjoyment of all human rights by older persons has called for the protection of older persons from violence.52

The Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination has also addressed the emergence of divisive narratives about war that impede peacebuilding.53 The Committee on the Rights of the Child recognizes that a culture of peace begins in the home, and it has highlighted the adoption by Brazil of its National Care Policy, “Growing up in Peace” Strategy and the draft national plan for family and community coexistence.54 The Working Group on discrimination against women and girls has drawn attention to the need to address gender discrimination, domestic violence and gender-based violence in an open manner, and to increase the number of women within the judiciary.55 Similarly, the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination has called for a public awareness campaign aimed at combating racial discrimination within society to be strengthened.56

The Special Rapporteur in the field of cultural rights has commended the creation of commissions for peace and understanding to promote dialogue.57 The Special Rapporteur on the rights of Indigenous Peoples has called for the inclusion of Indigenous Peoples in “total peace” policies.58

At the local level, nations that invest in creating institutions for peaceful dispute resolution implement solidarity to build internal peace. Examples include national peace ministries, committees or councils, labour tribunals or commissions, human rights commissions and local mediation councils. In Mexico, there are institutions addressing non-discrimination, such as the National Commission for the Study and Prevention of Drug-Related Crimes and the Consortium on Peace, Research, Education and Development. These institutions promote conciliation to address discrimination cases involving Indigenous Peoples, Mexicans of African descent, women, older persons, youth, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex persons and others. In Argentina, the Government provides social support for children, access to food for vulnerable people, maternal and infant healthcare, access to vaccinations, kindergartens, work programmes, and scholarships. In Colombia, progress has been made in three key areas that guide the efforts for total peace: the de-escalation of violence, territorial transformation and integrating members of armed groups into society. VIII. Civil society and solidarity for peace

In its submission, Pax Christi International stated that civil society and intermediary bodies were essential in advancing positive peace by strengthening democratic participation, promoting accountability and developing non-violent mechanisms for addressing conflict. However, in its submission, Women@thetable noted that one problem impeding solidarity for peace was fragmentation, given that most programmes address issues in silos: nuclear disarmament separately from gender equality, environmental protection separately from peace, and refugee rights separately from digital governance. Because peace requires holistic perspectives, it is essential to create networks of the different solidarity actors and understand their common challenges, such as the harassment of women environmental defenders.

In its submission, the Institute for Integrated Transitions described the concept of “horizontal peacebuilding”, in which translocal and interterritorial relationships and collaborations were prioritized and the role of “go-between” or mid-level peacebuilders was central. The Parents Circle – Families Forum brings together Israeli and Palestinian families who have lost loved ones to violence. Seeds of Peace brings together youth from regions in conflict for camps combining dialogue, leadership development and relationship-building.60 PeacePlayers uses basketball to bring together youth from divided communities in South Africa, Northern Ireland, the Middle East and elsewhere. The United Network of Young Peacebuilders brings together youth peace organizations globally. In India, the Ashoka Peace Innovation Network, the Mahatma Gandhi Peace Foundation and the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies conduct dialogue programmes, mediation training and non-violence education.61 The Niger has interreligious and inter-ethnic dialogues to promote solidarity for peace between communities.

In Kazakhstan, public councils, youth resource centres and friendship houses of the Assembly of the People host dialogue meetings, training sessions and educational seminars dedicated to issues of human rights, peaceful coexistence, prevention and prevention of radicalization, promotion of inclusive values and prevention of all forms of discrimination. Ecuador has a United Nations programme entitled “Constructing peace” to promote conflict prevention through dialogue. Dialogues with Indigenous Peoples are supported by the Conferencia Episcopal Ecuatoriana.

Associazione Comunità Papa Giovanni XXIII engages in non-violent peacebuilding in conflict zones in Colombia, Lebanon, Ukraine and the State of Palestine, among others, through Operazione Colomba, its peace corps, whose volunteers live alongside victims of violence and communities affected by conflict, providing a protective presence and promoting reconciliation. One of the association’s most significant initiatives is the campaign 59 Submission from Farhan Sahito. 60 Submissions from Juan D. Pierre, Madhav, N. Sewpal and Raissa Rambocus. 61 Submission from Shambhavi Kalash. for the establishment of a ministry of peace in Italy. 62 This campaign is aimed at institutionalizing peacebuilding as a central function of government policies. Several municipalities in Italy have already established peace departments. There is a global alliance of ministries of peace.63

In Nepal, civil society organizations have established parent self-help groups and community-based youth psychosocial support centres to strengthen local peacebuilding. These platforms facilitate peer support, conflict resolution and the inclusion of children with disabilities. Burkina Faso has a programme to support community conciliation with the participation of traditional and religious leaders, women and youth and provides psychological support and compensation to victims of violence, as well as counter-extremism programmes. It supports education on civic engagement aimed at reducing violence and drug use.

The International Dialogue Centre, the United Religions Initiative and local interfaith networks in South-East Asia and East Africa help reduce prejudice and build trust between communities. Community peace committees in Rwanda, the Fambul Tok model in Sierra Leone and the Centre for Peace and Conflict Studies in Cambodia demonstrate civil society leadership in mediation, trauma recovery and post-conflict processes.

In the Chiapas region of Mexico, community and faith-based organizations have developed participatory and non-violent methods to address conflicts linked to extractive industries. In Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, South Sudan and Uganda, Pax Christi International – International Catholic Peace Movement supports women religious leaders through training on active non-violence, trauma healing and peacebuilding, reinforcing community leadership in fragile contexts. In Colombia, the Pax Christi movement accompanies communities implementing the 2016 Final Agreement for Ending the Conflict and Building a Stable and Lasting Peace, including through platforms for dialogue between ex-combatants and Indigenous authorities, non-violence training for rural leaders and monitoring environmental obligations linked to land restitution and deforestation.64

In the Asia-Pacific region, the 2024 Nagasaki Catholic Peace Forum produced the Nagasaki Appeal for Peace, in which nuclear disarmament, youth leadership and ecological responsibility were explicitly linked. The training sessions strengthened capacity in peacebuilding, conflict resolution, trauma healing and the provision of support for vulnerable groups, particularly young people and women.

The Commissioner for Human Rights in Azerbaijan organizes a number of activities to promote the right to peace and security, including through the annual month of peace, aimed at promoting universal values and human rights, including the right to live in safety.

Despite the existence of these and many more initiatives around the world, peace solidarity activists are subject to surveillance, data-sharing with State actors, algorithmic flagging, discrimination, intimidation, online platform-enabled harassment, arbitrary detention, termination of employment, educational exclusion, violence, harassment, defunding, denial of banking services, economic exclusion, accusations of being foreign agents, prosecution under counter-terrorism, counter-extremist and separatist legislation, and assassination. Reopening the civic space around the world is essential. IX. Women as actors for international solidarity for peace

According to the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN-Women), in 2023, about 612 million women and girls lived within 50 kilometres of at least 1 of 170 armed conflicts, an increase of 41% since 2015. The United Nations has confirmed a 50% increase in cases of conflict-related sexual violence 62 See https://www.ministerodellapace.org/wpcontent/uploads/2018/09/CallingforMinistriesofPeace.pdf. 63 See https://gamip.org/. 64 Submission from Pax Christi International – International Catholic Peace Movement. since 2022, with women and girls suffering 95% of these crimes.65 Moreover, the levels of interpersonal violence, including domestic violence and child abuse, and suicide are far above levels of intercommunal violence around the world, underscoring the urgency of evaluating the focus of the international community in terms of safeguarding peace for women and children.66 In Brazil, the Maria da Penha Law, which created specialized mechanisms for preventing, protecting and prosecuting violence against women in domestic and family settings, serves as a model for other countries. Further, Brazil has the Women Living without Violence programme and the National Pact for the Prevention of Femicide. Mexico also has a law that is aimed at securing access for women to a life free of violence. It is complemented by the creation of women’s justice centres, shelters and a prevention programme.67

In several submissions, States referred to their national action plans implementing the women and peace and security resolutions in which the Security Council had called for the participation of women in peace processes, prevention and reconstruction.68 The Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom supports projects that enable women to pursue solidarity for peace initiatives, including those linked to disarmament or ecological justice. There are various organization of women peace mediators, such as: the Ibero-American Network of Women Mediators, the Regional Network of Mediators of the Southern Cone, the Nordic Women Mediators network, the Network of Women Mediators in Southern Africa, the Network of African Women in Conflict Prevention and Mediation and the Southeast Asia Women Peace Mediators. Similarly, the European Union supports the participation of women in peace processes.

In its article 10, the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa recognizes the right of women to participate in the promotion and maintenance of peace, peace education, conflict prevention and resolution, post-conflict reconstruction and rehabilitation. States Parties to the Protocol are to take the measures necessary to reduce military expenditure in favour of social development and the promotion of women. Under article 4 of the Protocol, States Parties are to actively promote peace education to eliminate gender-based violence.

In Argentina, programmes such as “Marcos de Paz” promote equality and women’s participation in conflict resolution. In El Salvador and Mexico there are projects that train women to be community leaders, defend human rights and serve as mediators.69 In Ethiopia, women-led movements, including Gender Empowerment Movement Tigray and survivorled networks, emphasize gender equality and justice as cornerstones of durable peace. Norway supports UN-Women in promoting the participation of women (including Indigenous women) in peace processes and governance in Africa, Latin America and Asia.70

In Yemen, since 2017, the Abductees’ Mothers Association has contributed to the release of over 650 forcibly disappeared civilians by facilitating local mediations between the parties to the conflict.71 The United Nations Development Programme supports additional programmes in Yemen to promote women’s increased participation in access to justice.72

In its submission, Women@thetable noted that the role of women in solidarity peacebuilding was everywhere but was either invisible or the subject of harassment and targeting. It called for greater recognition and inclusion of the solidarity for peace initiatives taken by women at the local level and suggested that women be included in digital transitional governance to consolidate sustainable peace. 65 See https://unstats.un.org/sdgs/gender-snapshot/2024/GenderSnapshot2024.pdf. 66 Anke Hoeffler and James D. Countries lack mechanisms for community-to-community solidarity that transcends State mediation; despite this, women’s networks across East Africa share violenceprevention strategies and peacebuilders in Colombia and the Philippines learn from each other’s approaches.

States reported in their submissions that they upheld solidarity with women and their right to peace through the adoption of national action plans to eliminate violence against women and gender equality action plans.73 In Argentina, feminist civil society actors network with different actors to identify and denounce gender violence, femicide and structural violence.74 In El Salvador, the Salvadoran Institute for the Advancement of Women works to prevent and identify violence against women and promote the economic autonomy of women. There is also a specialized tribunal aiming to ensure that women can live a life free from violence and discrimination. In Myanmar, women helped lead labour protest actions against the military Government.75 Guatemala has campaigns to prevent violence against women and the Indigenous Women’s Defenders Office engages in dialogues within communities to resolve disputes regarding the violation of women’s rights. Norway provides financial support to the United Nations Population Fund to promote the adoption of legislation prohibiting gender-based and domestic violence in Chile, Indonesia and Tajikistan.76 In the Syrian Arab Republic, in June 2025, a major conference on women’s rights and combating violence against women and girls brought together feminist organizations, youth groups and human rights activists to coordinate strategies for inclusive peacebuilding.

Brazil has three initiatives focused on women and youth. Empowering Refugee Women is focused on training women for inclusion in the Brazilian labour market. Strong Women is focused on entrepreneurship by empowering single mothers and female heads of household to achieve financial autonomy. Participants receive technical training, materials and financial assistance to launch small businesses. Youth in Action offers targeted training to young refugees and migrants.

Many civil society organizations actively act in solidarity for women’s rights, gender equality and non-violence, providing support services for survivors of domestic abuse, trafficking and discrimination. X. Culture of peace: solidarity for peace education and interfaith dialogue

Achieving peace requires the strengthening of social solidarity through the use of Indigenous traditions but also by promoting gender equality and anti-corruption norms.77 Non-violence, tolerance, mutual respect and intercultural and interfaith dialogue are essential elements of peace education. The rise in interfaith conflict in the form of terrorism, sectarian violence and societal division underscores the urgency of dialogue mechanisms to promote peaceful coexistence.

Peace education may be considered a means to instil confidence in youth to pursue life with a sense of purpose and connection to the world.78 Programmes should incorporate 73 See also https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2025-07/Beijing%2B30-From-words-to-actionNational-action-plans-to-end-violence-against-women-and-girls-en.pdf; and https://eige.europa.eu/gender-mainstreaming/tools-methods/gender-equality-actionplans?language_content_entity=en. 74 Submission from Fundación para la Democracia. 75 Tin Maung Htwe, “Paving the peaceful way of solidarity: the role of nonviolent labourers in Myanmar’s Spring Revolution”, Working Paper 3/2021 (Australian National University, 2022). 76 See https://www.regjeringen.no/no/dokumenter/handlingsplan-for-kvinners-rettigheter-arsrapport2024/id3145398/?ch=1. 77 Tim Murithi, “African approaches to building peace and social solidarity”, African Journal on Conflict Resolution, vol. 6, No. 2 (December 2007), pp. 9–33. 78 Lourdes R. In Argentina, the Peace and Justice Service and the Network of Public Educators provide peace education. The Foundation for International Democracy provides courses on bullying, cyberbullying and grooming. They promote empathy, solidarity and respect. Brazil has national human rights education guidelines that are focused on non-violence, empathy, respect for ethnic, racial, religious, gender, sexual orientation, gender-identity diversity and the peaceful resolution of conflicts.

Article 3 of the Constitution of Ecuador provides that the State has a duty to guarantee a culture of peace, comprehensive security and the right to live in democratic society free of corruption. Article 393 indicates that the State is to guarantee human safety through integrated policies and actions to secure peaceful coexistence, promote a culture of peace and prevent violence, discrimination and crime. The law on intercultural education promotes conflict prevention. The Ministry of Education seeks to eliminate discrimination in classes and promotes a culture of peace through bilingual education that highlights gender equality and respect for cultural diversity.

Article 3 of the Constitution of Mexico sets forth the aim of education as a culture for peace, and it has a national campaign for a culture of peace based on non-violence, tolerance of differences, mutual respect, empathy, intercultural and interreligious dialogue and gender equality, with the aim of fostering solidarity among groups, strengthening the social fabric through peace committees, community learning projects, human rights training and peaceful dispute-resolution workshops.

The law on growing together for the comprehensive protection of early childhood, childhood and adolescence in El Salvador seeks to secure access to quality education and includes provisions that promote a culture of peace and respect for diversity.

In Colombia, Act No. 1732 of 2014 on the Peace Education Chair is a legislative mandate requiring all educational institutions (preschool, primary and secondary) to implement a specific, mandatory curriculum focused on fostering a culture of peace, reconciliation and peaceful coexistence. The Ministry of Education has created an innovative programme incorporating elements of solidarity for peace, including restorative justice, anti-racism education and environmental education. Honduras has a national programme on education in human rights and the culture of peace, for public servants, government officials and the general public.

Togo has local peace committees and promotes peaceful dispute resolution in schools. In Ethiopia, community peacebuilding programmes in Tigray 80 illustrate that, when education connects to community healing, economic recovery and accountability, peace can begin to take hold. Ethiopian universities have worked with the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) to develop peace education curricula and teacher-training modules. The United Nations Children’s Fund has reported investments in Tigray education programmes designed to sow the seeds of peace and prosperity.

The Committee on the Rights of the Child has called for the adoption of peace education that would reject militarization, extremism, violence and discrimination and 79 See https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/what-you-need-know-about-social-and-emotional-learning. 80 See https://www.pactworld.org/blog/tigray-transition-communities-work-build-peace-andreconciliation. include prevention, early detection mechanisms, intervention protocols and psychosocial support for victims.81

The Organization of Islamic Cooperation promotes education that includes positive narratives of cultural diversity while emphasizing moderation, tolerance, compassion, justice and coexistence. It promotes interfaith and intercultural dialogue to foster mutual understanding.

Iraq offers peace education programmes disseminating non-violence, tolerance, mutual respect, empathy, intercultural and interreligious dialogue and gender equality to build solidarity between groups. Kazakhstan has projects aimed at fostering a culture of peace in the country’s educational and social institutions, as well as at the community level. Kazakhstan continues to support interfaith dialogue, including through the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions.

The Islamic Republic of Iran hosts intercultural and interfaith dialogue programmes, conducted through international and regional conferences. It reported in its submission that it provided free education for hundreds of thousands of Afghan children, which represented a significant step towards tolerance, mutual respect and the acceptance of diversity. These children study alongside Iranian students, fostering social cohesion and reducing cultural divides.

The Palestine Writes literature festival is devoted to the belief that art challenges repression and creates bonds between the State of Palestine and the rest of the world. Similarly, the Gaza Music Festival has showcased artists who use their platforms to advocate for rights for Palestinians. Visual art campaigns, such as Art for Gaza, have seen international artists create pieces that reflect the struggles of Gazan people, displayed in exhibitions globally. Additionally, social media campaigns featuring hashtags such as #ArtForPalestine allow artists and activists to share their work and messages of solidarity. These cultural movements not only raise awareness but also create a sense of community.

The Government of Azerbaijan has been taking measures to restore destroyed cultural and religious heritage sites in conflict-affected areas and ensuring safe access to them for returnees, thereby contributing to the culture of peace and tolerance in the country. Another important step forward is the establishment of contacts between civil society groups in both Armenia and Azerbaijan through visits and discussions aimed at building understanding at the societal level. The Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations of the European Commission and Plan International have focused on helping children in Azerbaijan remain in school.

In their submissions, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Guatemala stated that peace education was promoted systemically, including through bilingual education to promote mutual respect. In Nepal, peace education is considered to be most effective when emotional, social and structural dimensions of human development are integrated. 82 Collaboration between Government and civil society strengthens both individual resilience and collective harmony.

Associazione Comunità Papa Giovanni XXIII conducts peace education programmes in schools and local communities. Civil society also facilitates intercultural education and integration programmes for migrants and refugees. The University of La Plata in Argentina created an association of academics dedicated to the promotion of the human right to peace and its intrinsic connections to other human rights. It collaborates with the University of Mendoza, which has a course on peace education. XI. Right to truth and memorialization as an element of solidarity for peace

The right to truth may be considered a form of solidarity for peace after the commission of atrocity crimes. The validation of truth is a way of bringing peace to victims’ families and healing societies after conflict. In their submissions, States provided various examples of how they demonstrated solidarity for peace by supporting right to truth institutions and memorization initiatives.

In El Salvador, the National Commission on the Search for Persons who Disappeared during the Armed Conflict in El Salvador and the National Commission on the Search for Children Who Disappeared during the Internal Armed Conflict work with international forensic teams, investigate cases, find victims and reunite families. The State recognizes the contribution of women in searching for the disappeared in order to guarantee the right to the truth. In Mexico, women have engaged in solidarity actions to seek the truth about the enforced disappearance of women. In Guatemala, the Presidential Commission for Peace and Human Rights sponsors intergenerational dialogues on State violence and justice for victims. Azerbaijan seeks to identify the bodies of the deceased and to bring perpetrators to justice, which it recognizes as important for the right to truth for families and pertinent to peace and future reconciliation. In early 2025, a consortium of Syrian non-governmental organizations, in partnership with the International Center for Transitional Justice, conducted the first nationwide community dialogue since the end of the conflict. Those dialogues allowed victims, family members of the disappeared, civil society actors, local leaders and officials to share experiences and visions for justice.

It is a paradox that there is a contemporary trend of public order violence that occurs side by side with the establishment of truth commissions. These situations involve violations of procedural justice, arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance, torture and violations of other rights that require solidarity for the right to the truth to help restore peace.88 84 See https://upeace.org/. 85 See https://www.uio.no/studier/emner/jus/humanrights/JUS5134/. 86 See https://kroc.nd.edu/. 87 Submission from Whitestone. 88 See https://www.icj.org/el-salvador-crimes-against-humanity-within-the-framework-of-publicsecurity-policy/. XII. Conclusions and recommendations

The phenomenons of polarization and violence around the world signal the need to create a global coalition for solidarity for peace to promote mutual respect, recognition, trust, reconciliation and peaceful coexistence between groups that have been divided by ideology, disinformation or narratives promoting fear, hate, division and violence. The transformation of societies to incorporate sustainable social cohesion is necessary and requires taking back civic space from toxic actors in order to construct a united national identity based on the universal principles of non-discrimination and equality grounded in sustainable pro homine peace and solidarity. Moreover, full respect for peaceful dispute resolution should be confirmed as the fundamental procedural basis for inter-State relations to ground twenty-first century multilateralism.

States should: (a) Commit to twenty-first century multilateralism based on international solidarity for peace, strengthen multilateral forums for peacemaking and engage civil society, business actors, faith institutions, academics, schools and others in accepting common stewardship for peace, human rights and protection of the environment; (b) Fulfil the obligation of peaceful dispute resolution at the international, national and local levels; (c) Commit to preventive peace mediation, dialogue, inclusion, reconciliation and social cohesion strategies, including interfaith dialogue; (d) Establish ministries of peace that will promote inclusive positive peace policies supporting non-discrimination and equality; (e) Establish online dispute resolution platforms extending to digital labour technologies, with transnational coordination to manage jurisdiction issues; (f) Create rapid response solidarity mechanisms for mediation and preventive dialogue; (g) Support horizontal peacebuilding approaches between communities across different regions; (h) Invest in prevention, peacebuilding and policies to safeguard the environment; (i) Include community mediation networks, women’s cooperatives and local dialogue mechanisms in peacebuilding programmes; (j) Provide financial support to peacekeeping operations and right to truth and memorialization institutions; (k) Establish clear guidelines to eliminate cultural violence and prohibit speech promoting antisemitism, Islamophobia, misogyny and xenophobia and other incitements to discrimination or violence, in line with article 4 of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination and article 20 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; (l) Counter dehumanizing language and hate speech and protect asylumseekers, peace activists and humanitarian actors from doxxing and other attacks; (m) Strengthen civil society’s role in peacebuilding by supporting organizations engaged in reconciliation, coexistence and human rights consistent with universal values, while rejecting those that perpetuate division and violence; (n) Recognize the right of conscientious objection to military service and provide alternative service options and recognize the right to seek asylum based on conscientious objection to military service; (o) Desist from criminal prosecution of humanitarian actors engaged in the rescue at sea of asylum-seekers and migrants; (p) Guarantee the participation of women and youth in peace negotiations and peacebuilding processes, as well as digital governance; (q) Adopt specialized interpersonal violence policies to strengthen the prevention of and response to domestic abuse, femicide, child abuse and suicide; (r) Create community spaces for engagement in non-violent forms of solidarity, reconciliation and dialogue; (s) Support solidarity for peace education programmes in schools, universities and civil society institutions (including faith institutions) that foster non-violence, non-discrimination, tolerance of diversity, mutual respect, inclusion, intercultural and interfaith dialogue and gender equality; (t) Support the incorporation of social and emotional learning methodologies to promote the peaceful engagement of civic actors; (u) Ensure that solidarity for peace education includes truthful, historical accounts of apartheid and colonial or other forms of structural violence against minorities, Indigenous Peoples, women, refugees, migrants and others; (v) Integrate human security, disarmament and environmental justice as pillars of a shared solidarity for peace; (w) Implement article 7 (4) of the Arms Trade Treaty to prevent gender-based violence through arms export risk assessments; (x) Support ratification of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, end withdrawals from the Convention on the Prohibition of the Use, Stockpiling, Production and Transfer of Anti-Personnel Mines and on Their Destruction and continue arms control dialogues; (y) Ensure that actions to counter terrorism, extremism and transnational organized crime and to promote internal peace abide by human rights standards, including the right to participate in solidarity for peace actions, in accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Sustainable Development Goal 1689 and the Siracusa Principles.
